screens.title: Introduction to System Design and Interview Process
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this module we begin by defining system design and by walking through the interview process you will encounter. System design is the activity of composing components, interfaces, and data flows into a coherent architecture that satisfies both functional goals and non-functional constraints like scale and availability. In interviews, you are evaluated not by a single perfect answer but by how you gather requirements, structure a high-level design, dive into specifics, and justify trade-offs. During this lesson you will use the house-building analogy to practice clarifying requirements, sketching a high-level blueprint, and then drilling into plumbing or electrical subsystems as a focused deep dive. We will repeatedly pause to articulate trade-offs — for example, picking a database that favors availability at the cost of strict consistency — and practice phrasing those decisions clearly. You will also complete a short hands-on activity: deconstruct a simple To-Do List into functional and non-functional requirements. By the end, you should be able to run a structured interview flow that communicates trade-offs and an iterative plan for improvement. How will you change the way you ask clarifying questions next time you start a design problem?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define system design in clear terms, outline the typical stages of a system design interview, identify core attributes of a well-designed system, and explain why communication and trade-offs drive design decisions. First, you will learn to state what system design is and why it matters for large-scale software: it ties architecture to requirements and long-term maintainability. Second, you will be able to run a structured interview flow that begins with clarification, moves to a high-level sketch, then deep dives and concludes with monitoring and iterative improvements. Third, you will name and explain attributes such as scalability, reliability, and availability, and connect them to measurable expectations. Fourth, you will practice articulating trade-offs, showing how a choice that favors one non-functional requirement affects others. Each objective includes a short tactic you can apply in interviews: ask clarifying questions, draw a simple component map, pick a component to explore deeply, and summarize trade-offs. These skills matter because interviewers judge both technical depth and communication. How will you show each skill next time you design under pressure?

screens.title: Bloom's Path: Learn → Understand → Apply → Master
screens.narratorSegment: This page maps the skills you'll practice onto a learning progression. At the Learn stage you acquire vocabulary: what are functional and non-functional requirements, what components commonly appear in system sketches, and core attributes like scalability. At the Understand stage you link concepts: you explain how a load balancer, cache, and database interact to meet a requirement. At Apply, you practice by walking through an interview prompt, clarifying requirements and proposing a high-level design while defending choices. At Master, you communicate trade-offs fluently and propose iterative, measurable improvements. Each objective on this screen includes a short technique: a set of starter clarifying questions, a 5-component sketch pattern, a deep-dive checklist, and a template for a wrap-up summary. Practicing in this progression ensures you build both conceptual depth and the communication habits interviewers evaluate. When preparing, intentionally practice each stage on simple prompts — you will learn faster by iterating designs and reflecting on the trade-offs you made.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Bloom's Path

Bloom's Path: Learn → Understand → Apply → Master

A staged practice plan helps you move from vocabulary to fluent architecture decisions under pressure.

Learn
Memorize key terms and common components.
Understand
Relate components to requirements and metrics.
Apply
Run mock interviews and deep dives on a component.
Master
Explain trade-offs, performance, and future improvements.
Practice checklist
  • Ask 6 clarifying questions covering users, scale, latency targets, and failure modes.
  • Draw a 5-component sketch: client, LB, app servers, cache, database.
  • Pick one component and perform a deep dive for 6–8 minutes.
  • Summarize trade-offs and propose one incremental improvement.
Mini-mnemonic

Use the word C-H-A-R-T: Clarify, High-level, Analyze, Refine, Test — a checklist to run during interviews.

screens.title: What is System Design?
screens.narratorSegment: System design is the deliberate act of choosing components, their responsibilities, and the interfaces that connect them so the whole system meets specified requirements. In more concrete terms, a system design describes which parts will handle user requests, where state is stored, where caching occurs, and how data flows between services. This definition matters because good design ties technology choices to real needs: it balances performance, cost, and long-term maintainability. For example, when designing a To-Do List app, you decide whether to store items in a single relational table, place a small cache for recent lists, and how the client synchronizes offline changes. A common misconception is that system design equals picking tools. In reality, tools are downstream from clear requirements and trade-offs. You might choose a NoSQL store for scale, but only after you demonstrate why strong consistency is unnecessary for that use case. Key parts of a design include components (load balancers, app servers, data stores), interfaces (APIs, message queues), and operational aspects (monitoring, deployment, rollback plans). Always link components back to the requirement they satisfy. To check your understanding, try naming the single most important non-functional requirement for a system you use daily and explain how your architecture would meet it.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What is System Design?

What is System Design?

A concise definition and why it matters for real systems.

Core elements
Components, interfaces, data flows, and operational concerns like monitoring and deployment.
Concrete example
For a To-Do List you decide where items live, whether client sync is needed, and whether to cache recent lists for quick reads.
Misconception
Tool selection is not the starting point. Good design starts with requirements and trade-offs, then chooses tools to match them.
Key Takeaway

Design links requirements to architecture; always justify component choices by the requirement they satisfy.

Component checklist
  • Clients and API contracts
  • Load balancing and routing
  • Application servers and statelessness
  • Data stores and caching
  • Monitoring, deployment, and rollback
Guided reflection

Pick a service you use and name one component you would add or remove to improve its availability. Explain the trade-off.

screens.title: System Design Interview Stages
screens.narratorSegment: A predictable interview flow helps you stay organized and communicate clearly. First comes Clarification and Requirements Gathering: you ask about users, scale, latency targets, data durability, and constraints. This step prevents designing the wrong system. A concrete question set might include: expected daily active users, read versus write ratios, and uptime expectations. Next is High-Level Design where you sketch major components such as load balancers, application servers, caches, and databases to show how data flows. Keep this sketch simple and purpose-driven. Then choose one component for a Deep Dive — for example, the feed generation or the database schema. Here you show detailed algorithms, data models, and capacity estimates as relevant. After the deep dive, explicitly explain Trade-offs: discuss consistency versus availability, cache coherence, cost implications, and how choices match clarified requirements. Finally, Wrap-up by summarizing the design, listing monitoring needs and future improvements, and asking remaining questions. A common mistake is skipping clarification and jumping to a solution; avoid it. Practice this flow as a sequence so each step builds on the last, and you can defend every choice with a clear link to the requirements.

keyIdea.text: Run a five-step flow: clarify requirements, sketch high-level architecture, deep dive into a component, explain trade-offs, and wrap up with monitoring and improvements.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Interview Stages

System Design Interview Stages

Memorize and practice this five-step sequence so your answers are structured and defensible.

01 Clarify
Ask about users, scale, latency, and constraints. Example: expected daily users and peak traffic patterns.
02 High-Level
Sketch components and data flow: LB → app → cache → DB. Keep it simple and logical.
03 Deep Dive
Pick one subsystem to elaborate: API design, data model, or feed generation algorithm.
04 Trade-offs
Explicitly state compromises: consistency vs availability, cost vs latency.
05 Wrap-up
Summarize decisions, monitoring needs, and future improvements you would make.
Example: URL Shortener
Clarify: length of URLs, expected redirects per second. High-level: front-end, API layer, datastore. Deep dive: collision handling and key generation. Trade-offs: key length vs URL space. Wrap-up: monitoring redirects and cache hit rate.
Common mistake
Jumping into a diagram without clarifying assumptions. That often wastes time and leads to wrong priorities.

screens.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between functional and non-functional requirements is foundational. Functional requirements state what the system must do: user actions, A P I behavior, and data transformations. Examples include creating a to-do item, editing it, or listing user tasks. Non-functional requirements describe how well the system performs: scalability, availability, latency, throughput, and security. They determine the constraints that shape architecture choices. For instance, if the To-Do List must support millions of users concurrently, you will design for horizontal scaling, sharded storage, and aggressive caching. If the requirement is 99.9% availability, you will design redundancy and failover paths. A common misunderstanding is treating non-functional goals as optional extras — they are decisive. Another useful contrast: functional requirements often guide A P I and data models, while non-functional requirements guide component placement, replication, caching, and monitoring. When asked in an interview, always ask about both types: ask about expected users and latency targets together. To practice, list three functional and three non-functional requirements for a real service you use, then explain one architectural choice that arises from that non-functional requirement. Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements means functional requirements define behavior; non-functional requirements shape architecture and operational choices—both must be gathered early.. In practical terms, what the system must do versus how well it must perform. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Functional vs Non-Functional

Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements

Distinguish behavior from quality attributes and use both to guide decisions.

Functional requirements
  • Users can create, edit, and delete to-do items.
  • Users can list tasks and mark completion.
  • API returns appropriate status codes and validation errors.
Example
Implement POST /todos to create items with server-side timestamp and owner association.
Non-functional requirements
  • Availability target: 99.9% uptime.
  • Latency SLO: 100ms median for reads.
  • Support 100k concurrent users.
Architectural impact
High availability implies replication and failover; strict latency targets push caching and CDNs for reads.
Practice prompt
List 3 functional and 3 non-functional requirements for a note-taking app.
Misconception
Treating non-functional needs as optional leads to architectures that meet features but fail in production load.
Key Takeaway
Always ask for both functional and non-functional requirements; both steer design choices.

screens.title: Sketching a High-Level Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: A high-level sketch is a communicative tool: it shows major components and the flow of data without implementing every detail. Start with the actors and user paths, then add components that support those paths: front-end or clients, load balancers, stateless application servers, caches, databases, and auxiliary services like messaging or search. The sketch should map directly to requirements. For example, if low read latency is a requirement, include a cache between the app and database and explain TTL choices. If durability is critical, show replicated data stores and backup plans. Use simple arrows to indicate flow and annotate where state is kept. Do not attempt to show implementation details like S Q L schema at this stage. A useful heuristic is to ensure the sketch answers: how does a request enter the system, which components handle it, where is data read or written, and where are potential bottlenecks? A common interview mistake is over-detailing: a crowded diagram hides thought process. Instead, keep the sketch lean and be prepared to zoom into one component with capacity numbers, data shapes, and algorithmic choices on request. Try sketching a To-Do List high-level design in under three minutes, focusing on read and write paths and where caching helps.

keyIdea.text: Show actors, request path, core components, state locations, and likely bottlenecks — be concise and goal-driven.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › High-Level Design

Sketching a High-Level Architecture

Learn which components to include and how to keep the sketch focused.

Minimal component set
  • Clients / Load Balancer
  • Application servers (stateless)
  • Cache for hot reads
  • Primary datastore with replication
  • Messaging or background workers if needed
Example: To-Do List
Client → LB → App servers → Cache (recent lists) → Database. Background worker for periodic cleanup and backups.
Annotation checklist
  • Label where state is stored and whether it is replicated.
  • Note likely hotspots and mitigation (cache, sharding).
  • Identify failure domains and monitoring points.
Common mistake
Filling the sketch with implementation details instead of showing the flow and responsibilities.
Key Takeaway
A high-level sketch shows flow and responsibility. Keep it simple, then choose one area to expand with numbers and design details.

screens.title: How to Perform a Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: A deep dive is your chance to demonstrate depth and technical judgement. When the interviewer asks you to expand a component, pick a focused scope: A P I design, data modeling, indexing, caching strategy, or an algorithm such as feed generation. Start by restating the requirement you're addressing, then present the internal structure, data flow, and where performance constraints arise. Provide concrete design choices: data shapes, partition keys, cache TTLs, expected sizes, and capacity estimates. For example, diving into a To-Do List datastore you might explain a schema with user_id as the partition key, use of a write-through cache for recent lists, and an approach to paginate large lists. Include failure modes and mitigation: what happens when cache is stale or a shard fails. A common misconception is to present only one perfect solution; instead, present two alternatives and explain trade-offs: simpler schema with joins versus denormalized data for reads. End with performance numbers or scaling approaches so your choices feel grounded. Practicing deep dives with concrete numbers and alternative options will improve your ability to defend decisions under questioning.

keyIdea.title: Deep dive focus
keyIdea.text: Restate the requirement, show data model and flow, provide capacity reasoning, outline failure modes, and compare alternatives.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Deep Dive

How to Perform a Deep Dive

A structured approach helps you demonstrate technical depth and decision-making.

Step-by-step
  1. Restate the requirement and constraints.
  2. Show the internal structure or schema.
  3. Give capacity estimates and expected data sizes.
  4. Explain failure modes and mitigation.
  5. Offer alternatives and trade-offs.
Concrete example: To-Do List store
Schema: partition by user_id, sort by created_at. Cache: write-through for most recent 50 items. Scaling: shard by user hash. Failure: stale cache handled by cache invalidation on write; fallback to DB reads if cache miss.
Alternative A
Denormalized table for fast reads, higher storage usage.
Alternative B
Normalized schema with joins, better write efficiency but slower reads.
Key Takeaway
A deep dive should be concrete and measurable: include data shapes, load estimates, and failure handling. Compare options and justify your pick.

screens.title: Scalability, Reliability, and Availability
screens.narratorSegment: Three attributes repeatedly guide design decisions: scalability, reliability, and availability. Scalability is the system's ability to handle increased load by adding resources. It drives choices like horizontal partitioning, stateless services, and elastic infrastructure. Reliability is the probability that a system performs its intended function without failure over time; it motivates redundancy, retries, and careful error handling. Availability is the proportion of time the system remains accessible; to increase availability you design failover, replication, and graceful degradation. These attributes interact and sometimes conflict: increasing availability through replication may complicate consistency, and scaling reads with a cache may improve latency but introduces cache invalidation challenges affecting reliability. A typical interview task is to pick an attribute as the priority and map concrete design techniques to it. For example, to maximize availability for a read-heavy service you might replicate read replicas and use eventual consistency guarantees. A common misconception is treating these attributes as independent; good designers clearly state which attribute is primary and explain trade-offs for the others. When designing, always ask which attribute is most important for the user story you are solving.

keyIdea.title: Attributes mapping
keyIdea.text: Scalability, reliability, and availability shape architecture differently; prioritize one and explain trade-offs for the others.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Scalability & Reliability

Scalability, Reliability, and Availability

Know these attributes and their practical design implications.

Scalability
Add resources or partition data to handle growth. Techniques: sharding, stateless scaling, CDNs.
Reliability
Ensure systems do not silently fail. Techniques: retries with backoff, circuit breakers, and replication.
Availability
Keep the system reachable. Techniques: failover, multi-region deployments, graceful degradation.
Example trade-off
Choosing eventual consistency to improve availability may allow temporary stale reads. Explain why that is acceptable given the requirements.
Practice prompt
Pick a user story (e.g., timeline viewing) and state which attribute you would prioritize and why. Then list two design changes you would make to support it.
Key Takeaway
Explicitly prioritize system attributes in interviews and justify how your design choices support that priority.

screens.title: Explaining Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Trade-offs are central to system design. Every choice benefits some requirements while making others harder. The interview expects you to enumerate alternatives and explain the consequences. Start by naming the trade-off explicitly: for example, "I will choose eventual consistency to improve availability and reduce write latency, at the cost of temporary stale reads." Give a concrete comparison between two realistic options: a replicated S Q L primary-secondary setup versus a distributed NoSQL store. Discuss performance, consistency guarantees, operational complexity, and cost. Use numbers when possible: if reads are 90% of traffic, optimizing read latency with a cache makes sense. Also explain migration and rollback strategies: how would you revert a risky change? Interviewers appreciate when you list mitigations for the downsides of your choice. A common error is to pick the most fashionable technology without comparing alternatives against clarified requirements. Instead, present two or three shortlisted options and pick the best match with evidence. Finish by summarizing why your choice best aligns with the primary non-functional requirement you identified. This structure shows rigor and makes your reasoning easy to follow.

narration.text: Trade-offs are central to system design. Every choice benefits some requirements while making others harder. The interview expects you to enumerate alternatives and explain the consequences. Start by naming the trade-off explicitly: for example, "I will choose eventual consistency to improve availability and reduce write latency, at the cost of temporary stale reads." Give a concrete comparison between two realistic options: a replicated S Q L primary-secondary setup versus a distributed NoSQL store. Discuss performance, consistency guarantees, operational complexity, and cost. Use numbers when possible: if reads are 90% of traffic, optimizing read latency with a cache makes sense. Also explain migration and rollback strategies: how would you revert a risky change? Interviewers appreciate when you list mitigations for the downsides of your choice. A common error is to pick the most fashionable technology without comparing alternatives against clarified requirements. Instead, present two or three shortlisted options and pick the best match with evidence. Finish by summarizing why your choice best aligns with the primary non-functional requirement you identified. This structure shows rigor and makes your reasoning easy to follow.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off technique
keyIdea.text: Compare 2–3 options, state measurable impacts, propose mitigations, and tie the final choice to the prioritized requirement.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Explaining Trade-offs

Explaining Trade-offs

Make choices explicit and measurable; compare alternatives against requirements.

Comparison table
Option A: Replicated SQL - Strong consistency, higher operational complexity, good for transactional correctness. Option B: Distributed NoSQL - Better write scale, eventual consistency, simpler horizontal scaling.
Concrete numbers
If reads are 90% and target median read latency is 50ms, add cache with 80% hit rate to reduce DB load and meet SLOs. State expected QPS and per-node capacity when possible.
Mitigations
List rollback plans, feature flags, and canary deployments when proposing risky changes.
Common mistake
Picking a technology without comparing how it affects measurable requirements like latency or cost.
Key Takeaway
Always present alternatives, quantify impacts, and justify the selected option against the prioritized requirements.

screens.title: Iterate, Monitor, and Improve
screens.narratorSegment: Design is an iterative process. After proposing an architecture, discuss how you would monitor it, measure success, and evolve it. Monitoring shows whether your assumptions hold: track error rates, latency percentiles, cache hit rate, and capacity metrics. Use these measurements to propose incremental improvements like adding a cache, introducing read replicas, or sharding a hot table. In interviews, explicitly state metrics and thresholds: for example, if 95th percentile latency exceeds 300ms or error rate rises above 0.5% you will trigger an investigation and possibly roll back recent changes. Also discuss operational practices: automated deployments, blue-green or canary releases, and clear rollback criteria. A common misconception is that a design is judged only at time zero; interviewers want to hear how the system will evolve under real usage. Describe how you would run load tests, what signals would indicate the need for sharding, and how you would mitigate gradual scale increases. Showing an iterative plan demonstrates practical engineering judgement and an understanding that systems must be maintained and improved over time. Iterate, Monitor, and Improve means include monitoring, measurable thresholds, and a plan for incremental improvements to show practical, operational thinking.. In practical terms, design is never finished — plan monitoring and incremental changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Iterative Refinement

Iterate, Monitor, and Improve

Show how the system will be observed and evolved; include metrics and thresholds.

Monitoring signals
  • Latency: P50, P95, P99
  • Error rates and saturation metrics
  • Cache hit rates and DB queue lengths
  • Business metrics tied to system health
Action thresholds
Example: if P95 latency > 300ms or errors > 0.5% for 5 minutes, escalate and consider rollback or scaling actions.
Incremental improvements
Add cache, introduce read replicas, or shard tables as measured needs arise.
Deployment practices
Canary releases, feature flags, and clear rollback criteria reduce risk.
Key Takeaway
Design is iterative: define metrics, set thresholds, and plan small, measurable improvements that reduce risk while scaling the system.

screens.title: Hands-on: Deconstruct a To-Do List
screens.narratorSegment: Let's practice the activity from the chapter. You are designing a simple online To-Do List application. First, identify functional requirements: at minimum users should create new to-do items, list their tasks, and mark items complete. Optionally, allow editing and deleting. Next, identify non-functional requirements: decide availability targets, expected concurrent users, latency targets for reads, and data durability expectations. For example, a starter non-functional requirement could be 99.9% availability and median read latency under 100 milliseconds. Now connect one non-functional requirement to an architectural implication. If your availability target is high, you will design replication and failover, and ensure stateless application servers so traffic can fail over without state loss. If latency is the priority, include caching and consider read replicas or CDNs. A common mistake is to propose architecture without stating which non-functional requirement it addresses — always make the connection explicit. After listing requirements, sketch a minimal high-level design: client, load balancer, app servers, cache, and a replicated database. This practice builds the habit of linking requirements to components. In practical terms, practice listing 3–5 functional and non-functional requirements and one architectural implication. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › To-Do List Activity

Hands-on: Deconstruct a To-Do List

Practice stating requirements and mapping them to architecture choices.

Functional (starter)
  • Create new to-do items
  • List tasks for a user
  • Mark items complete
  • (Optional) Edit and delete items
Non-functional (starter)
  • Availability: 99.9%
  • Latency: median read under 100ms
  • Support 10k concurrent users
Architectural implication
High availability → replicated database, multiple app server instances behind a load balancer, and automated failover. Low read latency → cache recent lists with TTL and read replicas for scale.
Key Takeaway
Always state requirements first and then propose architecture that directly addresses them. Practice this habit often.

screens.title: Common Interview Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Interviewers often see recurring mistakes; recognizing them helps you avoid losing points. First, skipping clarification: jumping into a diagram without asking about scale, users, or latency results in a design that may not match expectations. Corrective strategy: always ask 4–6 clarifying questions. Second, over-detailing too early: drawing an enormous diagram hides your thought process. Correct: present a lean sketch and announce which area you will expand. Third, failing to discuss trade-offs: make choices without acknowledging their costs. Correct: state two alternatives and pick one with justification. Fourth, ignoring monitoring and operations: propose features but not how you will measure success. Correct: name 2–3 metrics and thresholds to monitor. Finally, being dogmatic about a favorite technology: interviewers expect reasoning, not loyalty. Correct: compare options and explain why one fits the clarified requirements better. In practice, rehearse a mock interview focusing on these corrections: ask clarifying questions, present a sketch, deep dive, compare alternatives, and finish with monitoring. This pattern is what interviewers are trained to evaluate. Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Common Mistakes

Common Interview Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

Short corrective tactics you can apply in interviews right away.

Mistake: No clarification
Always begin by asking about users, scale, latency, and failure expectations. This sets priorities for the entire design.
Mistake: Too much detail
Draw a simple sketch first. Announce the component you will deep dive into to show focused thinking.
Mistake: No trade-offs
State alternatives and pick one with measurable implications.
Mistake: No monitoring
Name metrics and thresholds you will watch post-deployment.
Key Takeaway
Fixable mistakes follow simple habits: ask, sketch, deep dive, compare, and monitor. Practice the sequence until it becomes natural.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's consolidate the most important ideas. First, system design is the practice of composing components and interfaces to satisfy functional and non-functional requirements. Second, the system design interview follows a flow: clarify requirements, sketch a high-level architecture, deep dive into a focused component, articulate trade-offs, and wrap up with monitoring and iterative improvements. Third, clearly differentiate functional requirements (what the system must do) from non-functional requirements (how well it must perform) and show how each requirement guides a design choice. When you practice, always link every architectural element back to a requirement and state trade-offs. These habits show both technical competence and communication skills, which interviewers value. Finally, you will be judged on your process as much as on your final diagram; demonstrate a disciplined flow and measurable reasoning. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this module we begin by defining system design and by walking through the interview process you will encounter. System design is the activity of composing components, interfaces, and data flows into a coherent architecture that satisfies both functional goals and non-functional constraints like scale and availability. In interviews, you are evaluated not by a single perfect answer but by how you gather requirements, structure a high-level design, dive into specifics, and justify trade-offs. During this lesson you will use the house-building analogy to practice clarifying requirements, sketching a high-level blueprint, and then drilling into plumbing or electrical subsystems as a focused deep dive. We will repeatedly pause to articulate trade-offs — for example, picking a database that favors availability at the cost of strict consistency — and practice phrasing those decisions clearly. You will also complete a short hands-on activity: deconstruct a simple To-Do List into functional and non-functional requirements. By the end, you should be able to run a structured interview flow that communicates trade-offs and an iterative plan for improvement. How will you change the way you ask clarifying questions next time you start a design problem?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define system design in clear terms, outline the typical stages of a system design interview, identify core attributes of a well-designed system, and explain why communication and trade-offs drive design decisions. First, you will learn to state what system design is and why it matters for large-scale software: it ties architecture to requirements and long-term maintainability. Second, you will be able to run a structured interview flow that begins with clarification, moves to a high-level sketch, then deep dives and concludes with monitoring and iterative improvements. Third, you will name and explain attributes such as scalability, reliability, and availability, and connect them to measurable expectations. Fourth, you will practice articulating trade-offs, showing how a choice that favors one non-functional requirement affects others. Each objective includes a short tactic you can apply in interviews: ask clarifying questions, draw a simple component map, pick a component to explore deeply, and summarize trade-offs. These skills matter because interviewers judge both technical depth and communication. How will you show each skill next time you design under pressure?

This page maps the skills you'll practice onto a learning progression. At the Learn stage you acquire vocabulary: what are functional and non-functional requirements, what components commonly appear in system sketches, and core attributes like scalability. At the Understand stage you link concepts: you explain how a load balancer, cache, and database interact to meet a requirement. At Apply, you practice by walking through an interview prompt, clarifying requirements and proposing a high-level design while defending choices. At Master, you communicate trade-offs fluently and propose iterative, measurable improvements. Each objective on this screen includes a short technique: a set of starter clarifying questions, a 5-component sketch pattern, a deep-dive checklist, and a template for a wrap-up summary. Practicing in this progression ensures you build both conceptual depth and the communication habits interviewers evaluate. When preparing, intentionally practice each stage on simple prompts — you will learn faster by iterating designs and reflecting on the trade-offs you made.

System design is the deliberate act of choosing components, their responsibilities, and the interfaces that connect them so the whole system meets specified requirements. In more concrete terms, a system design describes which parts will handle user requests, where state is stored, where caching occurs, and how data flows between services. This definition matters because good design ties technology choices to real needs: it balances performance, cost, and long-term maintainability. For example, when designing a To-Do List app, you decide whether to store items in a single relational table, place a small cache for recent lists, and how the client synchronizes offline changes. A common misconception is that system design equals picking tools. In reality, tools are downstream from clear requirements and trade-offs. You might choose a NoSQL store for scale, but only after you demonstrate why strong consistency is unnecessary for that use case. Key parts of a design include components (load balancers, app servers, data stores), interfaces (APIs, message queues), and operational aspects (monitoring, deployment, rollback plans). Always link components back to the requirement they satisfy. To check your understanding, try naming the single most important non-functional requirement for a system you use daily and explain how your architecture would meet it.

A predictable interview flow helps you stay organized and communicate clearly. First comes Clarification and Requirements Gathering: you ask about users, scale, latency targets, data durability, and constraints. This step prevents designing the wrong system. A concrete question set might include: expected daily active users, read versus write ratios, and uptime expectations. Next is High-Level Design where you sketch major components such as load balancers, application servers, caches, and databases to show how data flows. Keep this sketch simple and purpose-driven. Then choose one component for a Deep Dive — for example, the feed generation or the database schema. Here you show detailed algorithms, data models, and capacity estimates as relevant. After the deep dive, explicitly explain Trade-offs: discuss consistency versus availability, cache coherence, cost implications, and how choices match clarified requirements. Finally, Wrap-up by summarizing the design, listing monitoring needs and future improvements, and asking remaining questions. A common mistake is skipping clarification and jumping to a solution; avoid it. Practice this flow as a sequence so each step builds on the last, and you can defend every choice with a clear link to the requirements.

Understanding the difference between functional and non-functional requirements is foundational. Functional requirements state what the system must do: user actions, A P I behavior, and data transformations. Examples include creating a to-do item, editing it, or listing user tasks. Non-functional requirements describe how well the system performs: scalability, availability, latency, throughput, and security. They determine the constraints that shape architecture choices. For instance, if the To-Do List must support millions of users concurrently, you will design for horizontal scaling, sharded storage, and aggressive caching. If the requirement is 99.9% availability, you will design redundancy and failover paths. A common misunderstanding is treating non-functional goals as optional extras — they are decisive. Another useful contrast: functional requirements often guide A P I and data models, while non-functional requirements guide component placement, replication, caching, and monitoring. When asked in an interview, always ask about both types: ask about expected users and latency targets together. To practice, list three functional and three non-functional requirements for a real service you use, then explain one architectural choice that arises from that non-functional requirement. Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements means functional requirements define behavior; non-functional requirements shape architecture and operational choices—both must be gathered early.. In practical terms, what the system must do versus how well it must perform. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A high-level sketch is a communicative tool: it shows major components and the flow of data without implementing every detail. Start with the actors and user paths, then add components that support those paths: front-end or clients, load balancers, stateless application servers, caches, databases, and auxiliary services like messaging or search. The sketch should map directly to requirements. For example, if low read latency is a requirement, include a cache between the app and database and explain TTL choices. If durability is critical, show replicated data stores and backup plans. Use simple arrows to indicate flow and annotate where state is kept. Do not attempt to show implementation details like S Q L schema at this stage. A useful heuristic is to ensure the sketch answers: how does a request enter the system, which components handle it, where is data read or written, and where are potential bottlenecks? A common interview mistake is over-detailing: a crowded diagram hides thought process. Instead, keep the sketch lean and be prepared to zoom into one component with capacity numbers, data shapes, and algorithmic choices on request. Try sketching a To-Do List high-level design in under three minutes, focusing on read and write paths and where caching helps.

A deep dive is your chance to demonstrate depth and technical judgement. When the interviewer asks you to expand a component, pick a focused scope: A P I design, data modeling, indexing, caching strategy, or an algorithm such as feed generation. Start by restating the requirement you're addressing, then present the internal structure, data flow, and where performance constraints arise. Provide concrete design choices: data shapes, partition keys, cache TTLs, expected sizes, and capacity estimates. For example, diving into a To-Do List datastore you might explain a schema with user_id as the partition key, use of a write-through cache for recent lists, and an approach to paginate large lists. Include failure modes and mitigation: what happens when cache is stale or a shard fails. A common misconception is to present only one perfect solution; instead, present two alternatives and explain trade-offs: simpler schema with joins versus denormalized data for reads. End with performance numbers or scaling approaches so your choices feel grounded. Practicing deep dives with concrete numbers and alternative options will improve your ability to defend decisions under questioning.

Three attributes repeatedly guide design decisions: scalability, reliability, and availability. Scalability is the system's ability to handle increased load by adding resources. It drives choices like horizontal partitioning, stateless services, and elastic infrastructure. Reliability is the probability that a system performs its intended function without failure over time; it motivates redundancy, retries, and careful error handling. Availability is the proportion of time the system remains accessible; to increase availability you design failover, replication, and graceful degradation. These attributes interact and sometimes conflict: increasing availability through replication may complicate consistency, and scaling reads with a cache may improve latency but introduces cache invalidation challenges affecting reliability. A typical interview task is to pick an attribute as the priority and map concrete design techniques to it. For example, to maximize availability for a read-heavy service you might replicate read replicas and use eventual consistency guarantees. A common misconception is treating these attributes as independent; good designers clearly state which attribute is primary and explain trade-offs for the others. When designing, always ask which attribute is most important for the user story you are solving.

Trade-offs are central to system design. Every choice benefits some requirements while making others harder. The interview expects you to enumerate alternatives and explain the consequences. Start by naming the trade-off explicitly: for example, "I will choose eventual consistency to improve availability and reduce write latency, at the cost of temporary stale reads." Instead, present two or three shortlisted options and pick the best match with evidence. Finish by summarizing why your choice best aligns with the primary non-functional requirement you identified. This structure shows rigor and makes your reasoning easy to follow.

Also discuss operational practices: automated deployments, blue-green or canary releases, and clear rollback criteria. A common misconception is that a design is judged only at time zero; interviewers want to hear how the system will evolve under real usage. Describe how you would run load tests, what signals would indicate the need for sharding, and how you would mitigate gradual scale increases. Showing an iterative plan demonstrates practical engineering judgement and an understanding that systems must be maintained and improved over time. Interviewers often see recurring mistakes; recognizing them helps you avoid losing points. First, skipping clarification: jumping into a diagram without asking about scale, users, or latency results in a design that may not match expectations. Corrective strategy: always ask 4–6 clarifying questions. Second, over-detailing too early: drawing an enormous diagram hides your thought process. Correct: state two alternatives and pick one with justification. Fourth, ignoring monitoring and operations: propose features but not how you will measure success.
